Appendix K Proof for Partial Adoption by Attentive Agents

This section provides the complete proof for the case where a fraction of attentive agents adopt superior LLM technology while the remaining attentive agents learn from the equilibrium price. This case involves a rational expectations equilibrium with information feedback through prices.

Note on the Modeling Framework: This section adapts the main model’s framework to specifically analyze the case of learning from prices. In the main model (Section 3 and the preceding section of this appendix), predictability arises from different agents processing a single public signal with varying capacities—attentive agents extract precision τA=γA​τS\tau_{A}=\gamma_{A}\tau_{S} while LLMs extract τL=λ⁡(c,k)​τS\tau_{L}=\lambda(c,k)\tau_{S} from the same signal ss. To formally model a scenario where some agents can learn from the equilibrium price, it is necessary to introduce private information. A price based only on differential processing of public information would not convey any new information about the fundamental to agents who already observe that public signal—they could perfectly infer the noise component and learn nothing new.

Here, we operationalize the LLM’s superior capability as providing access to a private signal η\eta that represents information processed more quickly by LLMs and revealed publicly with a lag. This approach is conceptually consistent with the main model: an agent with a private signal has higher total information precision (i.e., τd+τA+τη\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\eta} vs. τd+τA\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}), which is economically equivalent to superior processing capacity. The private signal η\eta can be interpreted as complex information that sophisticated AI systems extract from news before it becomes obvious to all market participants—for example, subtle patterns in earnings reports or connections between disparate pieces of information. This modification allows for a tractable analysis of prices as a channel of information aggregation and learning, which is the central question for this extension.4040 40 An alternative interpretation: the private signal represents the output of a proprietary LLM model that some investors have exclusive access to in the short run, before the same analysis becomes widely available. This maps to our empirical setting where sophisticated investors may have deployed GPT-4 or similar models before they became publicly accessible.

K.1 Model Setup and Assumptions

K.1.1 Primitive Assumptions

Assumption K.1 (Market Structure).
  1. (i)

    The economy consists of a continuum of agents with total mass V>0V>0, partitioned into attentive agents (measure πA​V\pi_{A}V) and inattentive agents (measure πI​V=(1−πA)​V\pi_{I}V=(1-\pi_{A})V).

  2. (ii)

    All agents have CARA utility with risk aversion parameter α>0\alpha>0: U⁡(w)=−exp⁡(−α​w)U(w)=-\exp(-\alpha w).

  3. (iii)

    There exists a single risky asset in zero net supply with payoff d~\tilde{d}.

  4. (iv)

    Markets are competitive (agents are price-takers).

Assumption K.2 (Information Structure).
  1. (i)

    The asset payoff is d~=μd+σξ​ξ~\tilde{d}=\mu_{d}+\sigma_{\xi}\tilde{\xi}, where ξ~∼N⁡(0,1)\tilde{\xi}\sim N(0,1) is independent of all other random variables.

  2. (ii)

    The fundamental μd∼N⁡(d¯,σd2)\mu_{d}\sim N(\bar{d},\sigma_{d}^{2}) with precision τd=σd−2\tau_{d}=\sigma_{d}^{-2}.

  3. (iii)

    A public signal s=μd+εss=\mu_{d}+\varepsilon_{s} is revealed, where εs∼N⁡(0,σS2)\varepsilon_{s}\sim N(0,\sigma_{S}^{2}) with precision τS=σS−2\tau_{S}=\sigma_{S}^{-2}. This signal is observed by all agents in Period 1.

  4. (iv)

    In Period 1, LLM adopters gain exclusive access to an additional private signal η=μd+εη\eta=\mu_{d}+\varepsilon_{\eta}, where εη∼N⁡(0,ση2)\varepsilon_{\eta}\sim N(0,\sigma_{\eta}^{2}) with precision τη=ση−2\tau_{\eta}=\sigma_{\eta}^{-2}. This signal represents information that is processed more quickly by LLMs and is publicly revealed in Period 2 (see Assumption K.4).

  5. (v)

    Independence: The noise terms εs\varepsilon_{s} and εη\varepsilon_{\eta} are independent of each other and of μd\mu_{d}.

  6. (vi)

    Information processing capacities for the public signal are:

    τA\displaystyle\tau_{A} =γAτS,γA∈(0,1)(Attentive processing of public signal)\displaystyle=\gamma_{A}\tau_{S},\quad\gamma_{A}\in(0,1)\quad\text{(Attentive processing of public signal)} (168)
    τI\displaystyle\tau_{I} =ωτA,ω∈(0,1)(Inattentive processing of public signal)\displaystyle=\omega\tau_{A},\quad\omega\in(0,1)\quad\text{(Inattentive processing of public signal)} (169)
  7. (vii)

    The LLM’s superiority is captured by the precision of its private signal:

    τη=λ⁡(c,k)​τS\tau_{\eta}=\lambda(c,k)\tau_{S} (170)

    where λ:ℝ+2→[0,1]\lambda:\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2}\to[0,1] satisfies the regularity conditions in Assumption K.3. For LLM adopters with technology quality k>0k>0, the boundary conditions and monotonicity imply λ⁡(c,k)>0\lambda(c,k)>0, hence τη>0\tau_{\eta}>0. The restriction λ≤1\lambda\leq 1 ensures τη≤τS\tau_{\eta}\leq\tau_{S} (the private signal is no more precise than the raw public signal), a natural modeling choice though not essential for the equilibrium characterization. We assume attentive agents who adopt LLMs still process the public signal with precision τA\tau_{A}.

Assumption K.3 (LLM Technology).

The function λ⁡(c,k)\lambda(c,k), where kk represents the quality (e.g., model size) of the LLM technology and cc represents the complexity of the information being processed, is twice continuously differentiable with:

  1. (i)

    ∂λ∂k>0\frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial k}>0, ∂λ∂c≤0\frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial c}\leq 0 (monotonicity)

  2. (ii)

    ∂2λ∂k2≤0\frac{\partial^{2}\lambda}{\partial k^{2}}\leq 0, ∂2λ∂c2≤0\frac{\partial^{2}\lambda}{\partial c^{2}}\leq 0 (concavity)

  3. (iii)

    ∂2λ∂k​∂c>0\frac{\partial^{2}\lambda}{\partial k\partial c}>0 (complementarity)

  4. (iv)

    λ⁡(c,0)=0\lambda(c,0)=0 for all c≥0c\geq 0, and limk→∞λ⁡(c,k)=1\lim_{k\to\infty}\lambda(c,k)=1 for all c≥0c\geq 0

Assumption K.4 (Timing and Trading).
  1. (i)

    Period 0: No news, initial price p0=d¯p_{0}=\bar{d}.

  2. (ii)

    Period 1: Signal ss revealed, agents trade based on partial information processing, noise traders enter with aggregate demand u1∼N⁡(0,σu​12)u_{1}\sim N(0,\sigma_{u1}^{2}) (representing a continuum of small noise traders).

  3. (iii)

    Period 2: Full information processing. The private signal η\eta is publicly revealed as the raw signal μd+εη\mu_{d}+\varepsilon_{\eta}, where εη∼N⁡(0,ση2)\varepsilon_{\eta}\sim N(0,\sigma_{\eta}^{2}). By Period 2, information processing frictions lapse: all agents process the public signal ss at attentive precision τA\tau_{A} and observe η\eta. This yields a common posterior μL|s,η\mu_{L|s,\eta} with payoff variance σd,L2=TL−1+σξ2\sigma_{d,L}^{2}=T_{L}^{-1}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2}, where TL=τd+τA+τηT_{L}=\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\eta}. Agents retrade based on this unified information set, and noise traders enter with additional demand u2∼N⁡(0,σu​22)u_{2}\sim N(0,\sigma_{u2}^{2}).

  4. (iv)

    Period 3: Asset pays d~\tilde{d}.

  5. (v)

    Independence: Noise demands u1,u2u_{1},u_{2} are independent of (μd,s,η)(\mu_{d},s,\eta) and of each other.

Assumption K.5 (Inattentive Agent Behavior).

Inattentive agents:

  1. (i)

    Trade only on their noisy processing of the public signal ss (with precision τI\tau_{I}) and do not attempt to extract information from the equilibrium price p1p_{1}.

  2. (ii)

    Do not engage in speculative trading. They trade only based on the asset’s fundamental payoff d~\tilde{d} and do not anticipate retrading at price p2p_{2}.

This assumption reflects limited sophistication: inattentive agents lack both the information processing capacity to learn from prices and the strategic sophistication to engage in speculative arbitrage across periods. This behavior is consistent with models of noise traders or unsophisticated retail investors who trade on simple heuristics.

Note on Private Information and Noise Trading: A key feature of this equilibrium is that learning from prices requires two components: private information and noise. The private signal, η\eta, is essential because it introduces information into the market that is not common knowledge. Without it, the price would only be a function of the public signal ss and noise u1u_{1}. Any agent observing ss could perfectly infer the noise component, learning nothing new about the asset’s fundamental value.

The noise trading, u1u_{1}, is equally essential. It garbles the price signal, preventing the private information η\eta from being perfectly revealed. Without noise, the price would become a deterministic function of the signals, allowing non-adopters to deduce η\eta exactly (and thus match adopters’ information), eliminating the LLM adopters’ informational advantage. Together, private information and noise create a meaningful signal-extraction problem for non-adopting agents.

Units: The noise demands u1,u2u_{1},u_{2} are measured in shares, so the coefficient χ\chi in p1=a+b​s+g​η+χ​u1p_{1}=a+bs+g\eta+\chi u_{1} has units (price/share), ensuring (χ/g)​u1(\chi/g)u_{1} has the same units as η\eta.

K.2 Equilibrium Characterization

K.2.1 Bayesian Updating

Given their information, agent types form different posterior beliefs.

Lemma K.1 (Posterior Beliefs).
  1. (i)

    For an LLM-adopting agent (type LL) observing public signal ss (processed with precision τA\tau_{A}) and private signal η\eta (with precision τη\tau_{\eta}):

    μL|s,η\displaystyle\mu_{L|s,\eta} ≡E[d~|s,η]=d¯​τd+s​τA+η​τητd+τA+τη\displaystyle\equiv E[\tilde{d}|s,\eta]=\frac{\bar{d}\tau_{d}+s\tau_{A}+\eta\tau_{\eta}}{\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\eta}} (171)
    σμ,L|s,η2\displaystyle\sigma_{\mu,L|s,\eta}^{2} ≡Var[μd|s,η]=1τd+τA+τη\displaystyle\equiv Var[\mu_{d}|s,\eta]=\frac{1}{\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\eta}} (172)
  2. (ii)

    For an attentive, non-adopting agent (type AA) processing only the public signal ss with precision τA\tau_{A}:

    μA|s\displaystyle\mu_{A|s} ≡E[d~|s,τA]=d¯​τd+s​τAτd+τA\displaystyle\equiv E[\tilde{d}|s,\tau_{A}]=\frac{\bar{d}\tau_{d}+s\tau_{A}}{\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}} (173)
    σμ,A|s2\displaystyle\sigma_{\mu,A|s}^{2} ≡Var[μd|s,τA]=1τd+τA\displaystyle\equiv Var[\mu_{d}|s,\tau_{A}]=\frac{1}{\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}} (174)
  3. (iii)

    For an inattentive agent (type II) processing only the public signal ss with precision τI\tau_{I}:

    μI|s\displaystyle\mu_{I|s} ≡E[d~|s,τI]=d¯​τd+s​τIτd+τI\displaystyle\equiv E[\tilde{d}|s,\tau_{I}]=\frac{\bar{d}\tau_{d}+s\tau_{I}}{\tau_{d}+\tau_{I}} (175)
    σμ,I|s2\displaystyle\sigma_{\mu,I|s}^{2} ≡Var[μd|s,τI]=1τd+τI\displaystyle\equiv Var[\mu_{d}|s,\tau_{I}]=\frac{1}{\tau_{d}+\tau_{I}} (176)
  4. (iv)

    For any agent jj with information set ℐj\mathcal{I}_{j}, the posterior variance of the fundamental is σμ,j|ℐj2≡V​a​r​[μd|ℐj]\sigma_{\mu,j|\mathcal{I}_{j}}^{2}\equiv Var[\mu_{d}|\mathcal{I}_{j}]. The total conditional variance of the payoff is σd,j|ℐj2≡V​a​r​[d~|ℐj]=σμ,j|ℐj2+σξ2\sigma_{d,j|\mathcal{I}_{j}}^{2}\equiv Var[\tilde{d}|\mathcal{I}_{j}]=\sigma_{\mu,j|\mathcal{I}_{j}}^{2}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2}.

Proof.

Standard Bayesian updating with normal distributions. The posterior precision is the sum of the prior and signal precisions. The total variance includes both fundamental uncertainty and payoff noise. ∎

K.2.2 Key Definitions for Equilibrium Analysis

Definition K.1 (Precision Terms).

The following precision terms are used in the equilibrium characterization:

  1. (i)

    Fundamental precision after signals:

    TL\displaystyle T_{L} ≡τd+τA+τη(LLM adopters)\displaystyle\equiv\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\eta}\quad\text{(LLM adopters)} (177)
    TA∗\displaystyle T_{A^{*}} ≡τd+τA+τlearn(Attentive non-adopters after price learning)\displaystyle\equiv\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\text{learn}}\quad\text{(Attentive non-adopters after price learning)} (178)
    TI\displaystyle T_{I} ≡τd+τI(Inattentive agents)\displaystyle\equiv\tau_{d}+\tau_{I}\quad\text{(Inattentive agents)} (179)

    where τlearn\tau_{\text{learn}} is the precision of information about μd\mu_{d} extracted from the price (derived in the proof).

  2. (ii)

    Type-specific speculative precisions: Following the logic of the main model, speculative precision arises from the risk of trading against future noise. As established in Assumption K.4, by period 2 all agents trade on the unified information set (s,η)(s,\eta). The consensus expectation is therefore μL|s,η\mu_{L|s,\eta} with total payoff variance σd,L2=TL−1+σξ2\sigma_{d,L}^{2}=T_{L}^{-1}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2}. The period 2 price is thus p2=μL|s,η+(α/V)​σd,L2​u2p_{2}=\mu_{L|s,\eta}+(\alpha/V)\sigma_{d,L}^{2}u_{2}.

    For LLM adopters: Since they observe (s,η)(s,\eta), the uncertainty in the period 2 price arises solely from the future noise term u2u_{2}. The variance of the future price is V​a​r1​(p2|s,η)=((α/V)​σd,L2)2​σu​22Var_{1}(p_{2}|s,\eta)=((\alpha/V)\sigma_{d,L}^{2})^{2}\sigma_{u2}^{2}. Their speculative precision is:

    τp,L=V2α2​σu​22​(σd,L2)2\tau_{p,L}=\frac{V^{2}}{\alpha^{2}\sigma_{u2}^{2}(\sigma_{d,L}^{2})^{2}} (180)

    For non-adopting attentive agents: They observe (s,p1)(s,p_{1}) but not η\eta directly. Their uncertainty about p2p_{2} has two components: (a) uncertainty about μL|s,η\mu_{L|s,\eta} given their information, and (b) the noise u2u_{2}. Define the incremental uncertainty from the law of total variance:

    Δ≡V​a​r​(μL|s,η|s,p1)=V​a​r​(μd|s,p1)−V​a​r​(μd|s,η)=1TA∗−1TL≥0\Delta\equiv Var(\mu_{L|s,\eta}|s,p_{1})=Var(\mu_{d}|s,p_{1})-Var(\mu_{d}|s,\eta)=\frac{1}{T_{A^{*}}}-\frac{1}{T_{L}}\geq 0 (181)
  3. (iii)

    Effective trading precisions: From Lemma K.4, when agents can retrade and the price expectation is unbiased (E1​[p2]=E1​[d~]E_{1}[p_{2}]=E_{1}[\tilde{d}]), the optimal demand can be expressed using effective precision terms:

    LLM adopters: Their demand precision exhibits additive structure:

    τeff,L=σd,L−2+τp,L=(TL−1+σξ2)−1+τp,L\tau_{\text{eff},L}=\sigma_{d,L}^{-2}+\tau_{p,L}=(T_{L}^{-1}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2})^{-1}+\tau_{p,L} (182)

    Non-adopters: Their demand precision incorporates the parallel variance operator (a|b)≡(a−1+b−1)−1(a\,|\,b)\equiv(a^{-1}+b^{-1})^{-1}:

    τeff,A∗=[Δ+(Σp|σd,L2)]−1=[Δ+Σp​σd,L2Σp+σd,L2]−1\tau_{\text{eff},A^{*}}=\left[\Delta+(\Sigma_{p}\,|\,\sigma_{d,L}^{2})\right]^{-1}=\left[\Delta+\frac{\Sigma_{p}\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}{\Sigma_{p}+\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}\right]^{-1} (183)

    where Σp=τp,L−1\Sigma_{p}=\tau_{p,L}^{-1} is the variance of future price risk. This is derived in Lemma K.4.

    Inattentive agents: By Assumption K.5, they neither learn from prices nor engage in speculative trading:

    τeff,I=σd,I−2=(TI−1+σξ2)−1\tau_{\text{eff},I}=\sigma_{d,I}^{-2}=(T_{I}^{-1}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2})^{-1} (184)

K.3 The Case of Partial Adoption by Attentive Agents

Consider the case where fraction ϕ∈[0,1]\phi\in[0,1] of attentive agents adopt LLM technology, gaining access to a private signal η\eta with precision τη>0\tau_{\eta}>0. This gives them superior total information precision: TL=τd+τA+τη>τd+τAT_{L}=\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\eta}>\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}. The remaining (1−ϕ)(1-\phi) fraction of attentive agents do not have this signal but may infer it from the equilibrium price.

Economic Interpretation: This scenario captures a sophisticated market where some investors deploy advanced (e.g., proprietary LLM) technology, while others engage in price discovery to infer the conclusions of those advanced models. The learning-from-prices mechanism creates strategic complementarity: as more agents adopt LLMs, prices become more informative about their private signals, making non-adoption a potentially viable strategy and leading to a stable partial adoption equilibrium.

Definition K.2 (Rational Expectations Equilibrium with Learning).

An equilibrium consists of:

  1. (i)

    Price function P:ℝ3→ℝP:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R} mapping signals (s,η)(s,\eta) and noise u1u_{1} to price p1p_{1}

  2. (ii)

    Belief functions μj:ℝ2→ℝ\mu_{j}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} for each agent type jj

  3. (iii)

    Demand functions xj:ℝ2→ℝx_{j}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} for each agent type jj

such that markets clear and non-adopting attentive agents optimally extract information from prices.

Theorem 3 (Partial Adoption by Attentive with Learning).

Assume a fraction ϕ∈(0,1]\phi\in(0,1] of attentive agents adopt LLM technology, giving them a private signal η\eta with precision τη>0\tau_{\eta}>0. In a linear Rational Expectations Equilibrium:

  1. (i)

    The price function is p1=a+b​s+g​η+χ​u1p_{1}=a+bs+g\eta+\chi u_{1} where the coefficients (a,b,g,χ)(a,b,g,\chi) are determined by market clearing.

  2. (ii)

    Non-adopting attentive agents observe (s,p1)(s,p_{1}) and construct an effective signal about the fundamental μd\mu_{d}. Their updated fundamental precision is:

    TA∗=τd+τA+τlearnT_{A^{*}}=\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\text{learn}} (185)

    where τlearn=(ση2+(χ/g)2​σu​12)−1\tau_{\text{learn}}=(\sigma_{\eta}^{2}+(\chi/g)^{2}\sigma_{u1}^{2})^{-1} is the precision of the information about μd\mu_{d} extracted from the price. The noise-to-signal ratio has a closed-form expression: (χ/g)=α​TL/(V​mL​τeff,L​τη)(\chi/g)=\alpha T_{L}/(Vm_{L}\tau_{\text{eff},L}\tau_{\eta}), where TL=τd+τA+τηT_{L}=\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\eta}, τeff,L=σd,L−2+τp,L\tau_{\text{eff},L}=\sigma_{d,L}^{-2}+\tau_{p,L}, and mL=ϕ​πAm_{L}=\phi\pi_{A}, depending only on adopter-side objects and primitives.

  3. (iii)

    Market efficiency is increasing in the fraction of LLM adopters, ϕ\phi, and the quality of the LLM technology, τη\tau_{\eta}. We measure efficiency by the forecast variance Var⁡(μd∣s,p1)=1/TA∗\mathrm{Var}(\mu_{d}\mid s,p_{1})=1/T_{A^{*}}; thus efficiency increases if and only if TA∗T_{A^{*}} increases.

Proof.

Step 1: Price conjecture. Conjecture a linear price function of all random variables: p1=a+b​s+g​η+χ​u1p_{1}=a+bs+g\eta+\chi u_{1}.

Step 2: Information extraction by Non-Adopters. Non-adopting attentive agents observe the public signal ss and the price p1p_{1}. They know the conjectured form of the price function. They can then construct a new signal, zz, by isolating the parts of the price they do not already know:

z≡p1−a−b​sg=η+χg​u1z\equiv\frac{p_{1}-a-bs}{g}=\eta+\frac{\chi}{g}u_{1} (186)

This signal zz is a noisy measure of the LLM adopters’ private signal η\eta. Since η=μd+εη\eta=\mu_{d}+\varepsilon_{\eta}, the signal zz can be rewritten as a noisy signal about the fundamental μd\mu_{d}:

z=μd+εη+χg​u1z=\mu_{d}+\varepsilon_{\eta}+\frac{\chi}{g}u_{1} (187)

The total noise in this signal is εz=εη+χg​u1\varepsilon_{z}=\varepsilon_{\eta}+\frac{\chi}{g}u_{1}, which has a variance of V​a​r​(εz)=ση2+(χg)2​σu​12Var(\varepsilon_{z})=\sigma_{\eta}^{2}+(\frac{\chi}{g})^{2}\sigma_{u1}^{2}. The precision of the information about μd\mu_{d} that non-adopters can learn from the price is:

τlearn=1ση2+(χ/g)2​σu​12\tau_{\text{learn}}=\frac{1}{\sigma_{\eta}^{2}+(\chi/g)^{2}\sigma_{u1}^{2}} (188)

where χ/g\chi/g represents the noise-to-signal ratio in the price function, capturing how much noise trading affects the informativeness of prices relative to the private signal component.

Lemma K.2 (Bound on Learning Precision).

τlearn≤τη\tau_{\text{learn}}\leq\tau_{\eta}, with equality if and only if σu​12=0\sigma_{u1}^{2}=0 (no noise trading in Period 1).

Proof.

Immediate from the definition: τlearn=[ση2+(χ/g)2​σu​12]−1≤ση−2=τη\tau_{\text{learn}}=[\sigma_{\eta}^{2}+(\chi/g)^{2}\sigma_{u1}^{2}]^{-1}\leq\sigma_{\eta}^{-2}=\tau_{\eta}. ∎

The non-adopter now has an information set effectively equivalent to observing (s,z)(s,z). Their posterior belief about μd\mu_{d} is formed by combining the prior, the public signal ss (processed with precision τA\tau_{A}), and their inferred signal zz (which provides information about μd\mu_{d} with precision τlearn\tau_{\text{learn}}).

The non-adopter’s updated posterior mean and fundamental precision are:

μA∗|s,p\displaystyle\mu_{A^{*}|s,p} =d¯​τd+s​τA+z​τlearnTA∗\displaystyle=\frac{\bar{d}\tau_{d}+s\tau_{A}+z\tau_{\text{learn}}}{T_{A^{*}}} (189)
TA∗\displaystyle T_{A^{*}} =τd+τA+τlearn\displaystyle=\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\text{learn}} (190)

Key insight for closed-form solution: As shown in Step 5 below, the noise-to-signal ratio can be expressed as:

χg=α​TLV​mL​τeff,L​τη\frac{\chi}{g}=\frac{\alpha T_{L}}{Vm_{L}\tau_{\text{eff},L}\tau_{\eta}} (191)

where mL=ϕ​πAm_{L}=\phi\pi_{A} is the mass of LLM adopters and τeff,L=σd,L−2+τp,L\tau_{\text{eff},L}=\sigma_{d,L}^{-2}+\tau_{p,L}. Crucially, this ratio depends only on adopter-side objects and primitives, breaking what would otherwise be a circular dependence on non-adopter precisions. This allows us to compute τlearn\tau_{\text{learn}} in closed form before determining non-adopter demands.

Lemma K.3 (Gaussian Linear-Quadratic MGF).

If U∼N⁡(0,σ2)U\sim N(0,\sigma^{2}), then for any t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} and a>−1/σ2a>-1/\sigma^{2}:

E⁡[exp⁡(t​U−a2​U2)]=11+a​σ2​exp⁡(t2​σ22​(1+a​σ2))E\left[\exp\left(tU-\frac{a}{2}U^{2}\right)\right]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+a\sigma^{2}}}\exp\left(\frac{t^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2(1+a\sigma^{2})}\right) (192)
Proof.

Complete the square in the exponent and integrate the resulting Gaussian density. ∎

Lemma K.4 (Optimal Demand with Retrading).

Consider a CARA agent with risk aversion α\alpha who can trade at price p1p_{1} in Period 1 and retrade at random price p~2\tilde{p}_{2} in Period 2 before the asset pays dividend d~\tilde{d} in Period 3.

(i) When the agent observes all information in Period 1: If the agent’s Period-1 conditional expectation satisfies E1​[p2]=E1​[d~]=μE_{1}[p_{2}]=E_{1}[\tilde{d}]=\mu and the agent knows the Period-2 consensus, the optimal Period-1 demand exhibits additive precision structure:

x1=(τfundamental+τp)​μ−p1αx_{1}=\left(\tau_{\text{fundamental}}+\tau_{p}\right)\frac{\mu-p_{1}}{\alpha} (193)

where τfundamental=1/V​a​r1​(d~)\tau_{\text{fundamental}}=1/Var_{1}(\tilde{d}) and τp=1/V​a​r1​(p2)\tau_{p}=1/Var_{1}(p_{2}).

(ii) When the agent learns the consensus in Period 2: If the Period-2 consensus μL|s,η\mu_{L|s,\eta} is uncertain from the agent’s Period-1 perspective (with variance Δ>0\Delta>0), the optimal demand is:

x1=μA∗|s,p−p1α⁡[Δ+(Σp|σd,L2)]x_{1}=\frac{\mu_{A^{*}|s,p}-p_{1}}{\alpha\left[\Delta+(\Sigma_{p}\,|\,\sigma_{d,L}^{2})\right]} (194)

where (a|b)≡(a−1+b−1)−1(a\,|\,b)\equiv(a^{-1}+b^{-1})^{-1} is the parallel variance operator, Σp=τp−1\Sigma_{p}=\tau_{p}^{-1} is the variance of future price risk, and σd,L2\sigma_{d,L}^{2} is the Period-2 payoff variance.

Proof.

We solve by backward induction. The key challenge is that agents have heterogeneous information sets in Period 1, leading to different posterior beliefs and trading demands.

Case 1: LLM Adopters

For LLM adopters who observe (s,η)(s,\eta) in Period 1, the derivation follows standard backward induction with CARA-normal preferences:

  1. 1.

    Period 2 value function: Standard CARA-normal gives indirect value V2​(w2)=−exp⁡(−α​w2−12​(μL|s,η−p2)2σd,L2)V_{2}(w_{2})=-\exp(-\alpha w_{2}-\frac{1}{2}\frac{(\mu_{L|s,\eta}-p_{2})^{2}}{\sigma_{d,L}^{2}})

  2. 2.

    Period 1 optimization: The agent maximizes E1[V2(w~2)|s,η]E_{1}[V_{2}(\tilde{w}_{2})|s,\eta] where w~2=w1+x1​(p~2−p1)\tilde{w}_{2}=w_{1}+x_{1}(\tilde{p}_{2}-p_{1})

  3. 3.

    Quadratic expansion: The exponent becomes a⁡(x1)+b⁡(x1)​p~2+c​p~22a(x_{1})+b(x_{1})\tilde{p}_{2}+c\tilde{p}_{2}^{2} with:

    a⁡(x1)\displaystyle a(x_{1}) =α​p1​x1−μL|s,η22​σd,L2−α​w1\displaystyle=\alpha p_{1}x_{1}-\frac{\mu_{L|s,\eta}^{2}}{2\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}-\alpha w_{1}
    b⁡(x1)\displaystyle b(x_{1}) =μL|s,ησd,L2−α​x1\displaystyle=\frac{\mu_{L|s,\eta}}{\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}-\alpha x_{1}
    c\displaystyle c =−12​σd,L2\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}
  4. 4.

    Applying Lemma K.3: With p~2∼N⁡(μL|s,η,σp,L2)\tilde{p}_{2}\sim N(\mu_{L|s,\eta},\sigma_{p,L}^{2}) where σp,L2=1/τp,L\sigma_{p,L}^{2}=1/\tau_{p,L}, taking the FOC and solving yields:

    x1,L=(μL|s,η−p1)​(σd,L2+σp,L2)α​σp,L2​σd,L2=μL|s,η−p1α​σd,L2⏟Fundamental+μL|s,η−p1α​σp,L2⏟Speculativex_{1,L}=\frac{(\mu_{L|s,\eta}-p_{1})(\sigma_{d,L}^{2}+\sigma_{p,L}^{2})}{\alpha\sigma_{p,L}^{2}\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}=\underbrace{\frac{\mu_{L|s,\eta}-p_{1}}{\alpha\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}}_{\text{Fundamental}}+\underbrace{\frac{\mu_{L|s,\eta}-p_{1}}{\alpha\sigma_{p,L}^{2}}}_{\text{Speculative}} (195)

Case 2: Non-Adopting Attentive Agents

For non-adopters who observe (s,p1)(s,p_{1}) in Period 1 but learn η\eta in Period 2, the Period-2 consensus belief E2​[d~]=μL|s,ηE_{2}[\tilde{d}]=\mu_{L|s,\eta} is random from their Period-1 perspective. The key to solving this problem is to substitute the market-clearing law of motion for p2p_{2} before taking expectations.

Step 1: Market clearing in Period 2. From Assumption K.4, in Period 2 all agents observe (s,η)(s,\eta), yielding consensus μL|s,η\mu_{L|s,\eta} and variance σd,L2=TL−1+σξ2\sigma_{d,L}^{2}=T_{L}^{-1}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2}. Market clearing gives:

p2=μL|s,η+κ​u2,κ≡αV​σd,L2,u2∼N⁡(0,σu​22),u2⟂(μd,s,η)p_{2}=\mu_{L|s,\eta}+\kappa u_{2},\qquad\kappa\equiv\frac{\alpha}{V}\sigma_{d,L}^{2},\quad u_{2}\sim N(0,\sigma_{u2}^{2}),\quad u_{2}\perp(\mu_{d},s,\eta) (196)

Why this substitution is valid: The Period-2 market-clearing condition is an equilibrium outcome, not a choice variable. Since κ\kappa and the distribution of u2u_{2} are primitives (independent of agent A∗A^{*}’s Period-1 choice), we can substitute this law of motion into the agent’s Period-1 optimization without introducing circularity. The agent takes the stochastic relationship p2=μL|s,η+κ​u2p_{2}=\mu_{L|s,\eta}+\kappa u_{2} as given when choosing x1x_{1}.

Step 2: The key cancellation. Let μ≡μL|s,η\mu\equiv\mu_{L|s,\eta} denote the Period-2 consensus (random from Period-1 perspective). Substituting the market-clearing condition:

(μ−p2)2=(μ−(μ+κ​u2))2=κ2​u22(\mu-p_{2})^{2}=(\mu-(\mu+\kappa u_{2}))^{2}=\kappa^{2}u_{2}^{2} (197)

This eliminates both the μ2\mu^{2} term and the μ⋅p2\mu\cdot p_{2} cross term that would otherwise create a bivariate problem!

Step 3: Factorization. The Period-1 objective becomes:

maxx1E1[−exp(−α(w1+x1(μ+κu2−p1))−κ2​u222​σd,L2)|s,p1]\displaystyle\max_{x_{1}}E_{1}\left[-\exp\left(-\alpha(w_{1}+x_{1}(\mu+\kappa u_{2}-p_{1}))-\frac{\kappa^{2}u_{2}^{2}}{2\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}\right)\bigg|s,p_{1}\right] (198)

The exponent is linear in μ\mu and quadratic in u2u_{2}. Since μ⟂u2\mu\perp u_{2}, the expectation factorizes:

e−α⁡(w1−x1​p1)⋅E1[e−α​x1​μ|s,p1]⏟μ​-part⋅E⁡[e−α​x1​κ​u2−κ2​u22/(2​σd,L2)]⏟u2​-parte^{-\alpha(w_{1}-x_{1}p_{1})}\cdot\underbrace{E_{1}[e^{-\alpha x_{1}\mu}|s,p_{1}]}_{\mu\text{-part}}\cdot\underbrace{E[e^{-\alpha x_{1}\kappa u_{2}-\kappa^{2}u_{2}^{2}/(2\sigma_{d,L}^{2})}]}_{u_{2}\text{-part}} (199)

Step 4: Computing the expectations. From the non-adopter’s Period-1 perspective:

  • •

    μ|(s,p1)∼N⁡(μp,Δ)\mu\mid(s,p_{1})\sim N(\mu_{p},\Delta) where μp=E1[μL|s,η|s,p1]=μA∗|s,p\mu_{p}=E_{1}[\mu_{L|s,\eta}|s,p_{1}]=\mu_{A^{*}|s,p} and Δ=V​a​r1​(μL|s,η|s,p1)=TA∗−1−TL−1≥0\Delta=Var_{1}(\mu_{L|s,\eta}|s,p_{1})=T_{A^{*}}^{-1}-T_{L}^{-1}\geq 0

  • •

    u2∼N⁡(0,σu​22)u_{2}\sim N(0,\sigma_{u2}^{2}) independent of all Period-1 information

Using standard MGFs for univariate normals:

E1[e−α​x1​μ|s,p1]\displaystyle E_{1}[e^{-\alpha x_{1}\mu}|s,p_{1}] =exp⁡(−α​x1​μp+α2​x12​Δ2)\displaystyle=\exp\left(-\alpha x_{1}\mu_{p}+\frac{\alpha^{2}x_{1}^{2}\Delta}{2}\right) (200)
E⁡[e−α​x1​κ​u2−κ2​u22/(2​σd,L2)]\displaystyle E[e^{-\alpha x_{1}\kappa u_{2}-\kappa^{2}u_{2}^{2}/(2\sigma_{d,L}^{2})}] =11+Σp/σd,L2​exp⁡(α2​x12​Σp2​(1+Σp/σd,L2))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\Sigma_{p}/\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}}\exp\left(\frac{\alpha^{2}x_{1}^{2}\Sigma_{p}}{2(1+\Sigma_{p}/\sigma_{d,L}^{2})}\right) (201)

where Σp≡κ2​σu​22=(αV​σd,L2)2​σu​22=1/τp,L\Sigma_{p}\equiv\kappa^{2}\sigma_{u2}^{2}=\left(\frac{\alpha}{V}\sigma_{d,L}^{2}\right)^{2}\sigma_{u2}^{2}=1/\tau_{p,L}.

ℒ⁡(x1)=α​x1​(p1−μp)+α2​x122​[Δ+Σp1+Σp/σd,L2]\mathcal{L}(x_{1})=\alpha x_{1}(p_{1}-\mu_{p})+\frac{\alpha^{2}x_{1}^{2}}{2}\left[\Delta+\frac{\Sigma_{p}}{1+\Sigma_{p}/\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}\right] (202)

Define the parallel variance operator (a|b)≡(a−1+b−1)−1(a\,|\,b)\equiv(a^{-1}+b^{-1})^{-1} (the variance of two independent Gaussian risks borne in parallel) and the effective variance:

σeff2≡Δ+(Σp|σd,L2)=Δ+Σp​σd,L2Σp+σd,L2\sigma_{\text{eff}}^{2}\equiv\Delta+(\Sigma_{p}\,|\,\sigma_{d,L}^{2})=\Delta+\frac{\Sigma_{p}\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}{\Sigma_{p}+\sigma_{d,L}^{2}} (203)

The independence u2⟂(μd,s,η)u_{2}\perp(\mu_{d},s,\eta) allows the expectation to factorize, yielding a closed-form solution.

Taking the FOC: d​ℒd​x1=α⁡(p1−μp)+α2​x1​σeff2=0\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dx_{1}}=\alpha(p_{1}-\mu_{p})+\alpha^{2}x_{1}\sigma_{\text{eff}}^{2}=0, yielding:

x1,A∗=μp−p1α​σeff2=μA∗|s,p−p1α⁡[Δ+(Σp|σd,L2)]\boxed{x_{1,A^{*}}=\frac{\mu_{p}-p_{1}}{\alpha\sigma_{\text{eff}}^{2}}=\frac{\mu_{A^{*}|s,p}-p_{1}}{\alpha\left[\Delta+(\Sigma_{p}\,|\,\sigma_{d,L}^{2})\right]}} (204)

General Result

The demand formulas for all agent types are:

  • •

    LLM adopters (Δ=0\Delta=0):

    x1,L=(σd,L−2+τp,L)​μL|s,η−p1αx_{1,L}=\left(\sigma_{d,L}^{-2}+\tau_{p,L}\right)\frac{\mu_{L|s,\eta}-p_{1}}{\alpha} (205)
  • •

    Non-adopters (Δ=TA∗−1−TL−1≥0\Delta=T_{A^{*}}^{-1}-T_{L}^{-1}\geq 0):

    x1,A∗=μA∗|s,p−p1α⁡[Δ+(Σp|σd,L2)]x_{1,A^{*}}=\frac{\mu_{A^{*}|s,p}-p_{1}}{\alpha\left[\Delta+(\Sigma_{p}\,|\,\sigma_{d,L}^{2})\right]} (206)
  • •

    Inattentive agents: Only fundamental component (no speculation), x1,I=μI|s−p1α​σd,I2x_{1,I}=\frac{\mu_{I|s}-p_{1}}{\alpha\sigma_{d,I}^{2}}

where Σp=τp,L−1=(α/V)2​(σd,L2)2​σu​22\Sigma_{p}=\tau_{p,L}^{-1}=(\alpha/V)^{2}(\sigma_{d,L}^{2})^{2}\sigma_{u2}^{2} is the variance of future price risk and (a|b)=(a−1+b−1)−1(a\,|\,b)=(a^{-1}+b^{-1})^{-1} is the parallel variance operator. ∎

Step 3: Demands. All agents form their demands based on their information, as derived in Lemma K.4.

For LLM adopters, since E1[d~|s,η]=E1[p2|s,η]=μL|s,ηE_{1}[\tilde{d}|s,\eta]=E_{1}[p_{2}|s,\eta]=\mu_{L|s,\eta}:

xL=(σd,L−2+τp,L)​μL|s,η−p1αx_{L}=\left(\sigma_{d,L}^{-2}+\tau_{p,L}\right)\frac{\mu_{L|s,\eta}-p_{1}}{\alpha} (207)

where σd,L2=TL−1+σξ2\sigma_{d,L}^{2}=T_{L}^{-1}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2} and τp,L=V2/(α2​σu​22​(σd,L2)2)\tau_{p,L}=V^{2}/(\alpha^{2}\sigma_{u2}^{2}(\sigma_{d,L}^{2})^{2}).

For non-adopters, their demand incorporates the additional uncertainty Δ=TA∗−1−TL−1\Delta=T_{A^{*}}^{-1}-T_{L}^{-1} about the Period-2 consensus:

xA∗=μA∗|s,p−p1α⁡[Δ+(Σp|σd,L2)]x_{A^{*}}=\frac{\mu_{A^{*}|s,p}-p_{1}}{\alpha\left[\Delta+(\Sigma_{p}\,|\,\sigma_{d,L}^{2})\right]} (208)

where Σp=τp,L−1\Sigma_{p}=\tau_{p,L}^{-1} and (a|b)=(a−1+b−1)−1(a\,|\,b)=(a^{-1}+b^{-1})^{-1} is the parallel variance operator.

For inattentive agents, by Assumption K.5, they neither learn from prices nor engage in speculative trading:

xI=σd,I−2​μI|s−p1αx_{I}=\sigma_{d,I}^{-2}\frac{\mu_{I|s}-p_{1}}{\alpha} (209)

where σd,I2=TI−1+σξ2\sigma_{d,I}^{2}=T_{I}^{-1}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2}.

mL​V⋅xL+mA​V⋅xA∗+mI​V⋅xI=−u1m_{L}V\cdot x_{L}+m_{A}V\cdot x_{A^{*}}+m_{I}V\cdot x_{I}=-u_{1} (210)

Substituting the demand functions from Step 3 and solving for p1p_{1} yields a linear price function. Define effective precision weights:

τeff,L\displaystyle\tau_{\text{eff},L} ≡σd,L−2+τp,L\displaystyle\equiv\sigma_{d,L}^{-2}+\tau_{p,L} (211)
τeff,A∗\displaystyle\tau_{\text{eff},A^{*}} ≡[Δ+(Σp|σd,L2)]−1\displaystyle\equiv\left[\Delta+(\Sigma_{p}\,|\,\sigma_{d,L}^{2})\right]^{-1} (212)
τeff,I\displaystyle\tau_{\text{eff},I} ≡σd,I−2\displaystyle\equiv\sigma_{d,I}^{-2} (213)

Define the aggregate effective precision mass:

S≡mL​τeff,L+mA​τeff,A∗+mI​τeff,IS\equiv m_{L}\tau_{\text{eff},L}+m_{A}\tau_{\text{eff},A^{*}}+m_{I}\tau_{\text{eff},I} (214)

and precision-weighted masses wj=mj​τeff,j/Sw_{j}=m_{j}\tau_{\text{eff},j}/S for j∈{L,A∗,I}j\in\{L,A^{*},I\}. Then:

p1=∑j∈{L,A∗,I}wj​μj+αV​S​u1p_{1}=\sum_{j\in\{L,A^{*},I\}}w_{j}\mu_{j}+\frac{\alpha}{VS}u_{1} (215)

where μL=μL|s,η\mu_{L}=\mu_{L|s,\eta}, μA∗=μA∗|s,p\mu_{A^{*}}=\mu_{A^{*}|s,p}, and μI=μI|s\mu_{I}=\mu_{I|s}.

Remark (Existence and uniqueness of linear REE).

For ϕ>0\phi>0, τη>0\tau_{\eta}>0, and finite σu​12,σu​22\sigma_{u1}^{2},\sigma_{u2}^{2}, a linear REE exists and is unique.

Existence follows from the constructive sequence: adopters’ objects ⇒\Rightarrow the ratio

χg=α​TLV​mL​τeff,L​τη\frac{\chi}{g}=\frac{\alpha T_{L}}{Vm_{L}\tau_{\text{eff},L}\tau_{\eta}}

(depends only on adopter-side primitives) ⇒\Rightarrow τlearn\tau_{\text{learn}}, TA∗T_{A^{*}}, SS, wjw_{j} ⇒\Rightarrow (a,b,g,χ)(a,b,g,\chi). Well-posedness requires S>0S>0 (satisfied because each τeff,j>0\tau_{\text{eff},j}>0 under finite variances) and g>0g>0 (satisfied because κη>0\kappa_{\eta}>0 when mL>0m_{L}>0 and τη>0\tau_{\eta}>0).

Uniqueness holds because any linear REE must satisfy the same coefficient-matching, which forces the same unique χ/g\chi/g, hence the same τlearn\tau_{\text{learn}}, TA∗T_{A^{*}}, SS, wjw_{j}, and therefore the same (a,b,g,χ)(a,b,g,\chi).

Economic intuition: Adopters’ trading against noise pins the price’s informativeness (χ/g\chi/g). Once that ratio is fixed, what non-adopters can learn, their risk, their demand, and therefore the entire price—all become determinate. This mirrors the standard CARA–Gaussian linear-REE uniqueness logic [36, 30], with the refinement that the key fixed point collapses to the single ratio χ/g\chi/g, which we solve in closed form.

Step 5: Solving for price coefficients. Substituting the expressions for posterior means:

μL\displaystyle\mu_{L} =τd​d¯+τA​s+τη​ηTL\displaystyle=\frac{\tau_{d}\bar{d}+\tau_{A}s+\tau_{\eta}\eta}{T_{L}} (216)
μA∗\displaystyle\mu_{A^{*}} =τd​d¯+τA​s+τlearn​zTA∗,z=p1−a−b​sg\displaystyle=\frac{\tau_{d}\bar{d}+\tau_{A}s+\tau_{\text{learn}}z}{T_{A^{*}}},\quad z=\frac{p_{1}-a-bs}{g} (217)
μI\displaystyle\mu_{I} =τd​d¯+τI​sTI\displaystyle=\frac{\tau_{d}\bar{d}+\tau_{I}s}{T_{I}} (218)

Matching coefficients with p1=a+b​s+g​η+χ​u1p_{1}=a+bs+g\eta+\chi u_{1} gives:

a\displaystyle a =(wL​τdTL+wA∗​τdTA∗+wI​τdTI)​d¯\displaystyle=\left(\frac{w_{L}\tau_{d}}{T_{L}}+\frac{w_{A^{*}}\tau_{d}}{T_{A^{*}}}+\frac{w_{I}\tau_{d}}{T_{I}}\right)\bar{d} (219)
b\displaystyle b =wL​τATL+wA∗​τATA∗+wI​τITI\displaystyle=\frac{w_{L}\tau_{A}}{T_{L}}+\frac{w_{A^{*}}\tau_{A}}{T_{A^{*}}}+\frac{w_{I}\tau_{I}}{T_{I}} (220)

For the coefficients on η\eta and u1u_{1}, define:

κη\displaystyle\kappa_{\eta} ≡wL​τηTL,κA≡wA∗​τlearnTA∗,κu0≡αV​S\displaystyle\equiv\frac{w_{L}\tau_{\eta}}{T_{L}},\quad\kappa_{A}\equiv\frac{w_{A^{*}}\tau_{\text{learn}}}{T_{A^{*}}},\quad\kappa_{u}^{0}\equiv\frac{\alpha}{VS} (221)

Collecting terms yields:

g\displaystyle g =κη+κA(η-coefficient: adopters and non-adopters)\displaystyle=\kappa_{\eta}+\kappa_{A}\quad\text{($\eta$-coefficient: adopters and non-adopters)} (222)
χ\displaystyle\chi =κA(χg)+κu0(u1-coefficient: direct and learned channels)\displaystyle=\kappa_{A}\left(\frac{\chi}{g}\right)+\kappa_{u}^{0}\quad\text{($u_{1}$-coefficient: direct and learned channels)} (223)

Key algebraic simplification: Dividing the η\eta-coefficient by the u1u_{1}-coefficient immediately yields the noise-to-signal ratio:

χg=κu0κη=α​TLV​mL​τeff,L​τη\boxed{\frac{\chi}{g}=\frac{\kappa_{u}^{0}}{\kappa_{\eta}}=\frac{\alpha T_{L}}{Vm_{L}\tau_{\text{eff},L}\tau_{\eta}}} (224)

Why this works: From the second equation, χ=κA​(χ/g)+κu0\chi=\kappa_{A}(\chi/g)+\kappa_{u}^{0}, rearranging gives χ⁡(1−κA/g)=κu0\chi(1-\kappa_{A}/g)=\kappa_{u}^{0}. Since g=κη+κAg=\kappa_{\eta}+\kappa_{A}, we have 1−κA/g=κη/g1-\kappa_{A}/g=\kappa_{\eta}/g, so χ/g=κu0/κη\chi/g=\kappa_{u}^{0}/\kappa_{\eta}. The κA\kappa_{A} terms—reflecting non-adopter behavior—cancel perfectly in the ratio. The aggregate precision SS also cancels. This holds regardless of the specific non-adopter demand formula.

Economic interpretation: The noise-to-signal ratio—the measure of price informativeness—is determined entirely by LLM adopters’ behavior. Non-adopters are ”price-takers” in two senses: they take p1p_{1} as given, and they take the informativeness of p1p_{1} (captured by χ/g\chi/g) as given. The informativeness is created by LLM adopters trading on η\eta against noise u1u_{1}; non-adopters’ trades merely scale both gg and χ\chi proportionally, leaving χ/g\chi/g unchanged.

Therefore, χ/g\chi/g depends only on:

  • •

    Primitives: α,V,τd,τA,τη,ϕ,πA,σξ2,σu​22\alpha,V,\tau_{d},\tau_{A},\tau_{\eta},\phi,\pi_{A},\sigma_{\xi}^{2},\sigma_{u2}^{2}

  • •

    Adopter-side objects: TL=τd+τA+τηT_{L}=\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\eta} and τeff,L=σd,L−2+τp,L\tau_{\text{eff},L}=\sigma_{d,L}^{-2}+\tau_{p,L}

This breaks the circularity and allows closed-form solution without iteration.

The individual coefficients can be computed from the weights, but are not needed for the main result. The key is that the ratio χ/g\chi/g depends only on adopter-side primitives.

Closed-form solution procedure:

  1. 1.

    Compute adopter objects:

    TL\displaystyle T_{L} =τd+τA+τη\displaystyle=\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\eta}
    σd,L2\displaystyle\sigma_{d,L}^{2} =TL−1+σξ2\displaystyle=T_{L}^{-1}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2}
    τp,L\displaystyle\tau_{p,L} =V2α2​σu​22​(σd,L2)2\displaystyle=\frac{V^{2}}{\alpha^{2}\sigma_{u2}^{2}(\sigma_{d,L}^{2})^{2}}
    τeff,L\displaystyle\tau_{\text{eff},L} =σd,L−2+τp,L\displaystyle=\sigma_{d,L}^{-2}+\tau_{p,L}
  2. 2.

    Compute learning precision:

    τlearn=[ση2+(α​TLV​mL​τeff,L​τη)2​σu​12]−1\tau_{\text{learn}}=\left[\sigma_{\eta}^{2}+\left(\frac{\alpha T_{L}}{Vm_{L}\tau_{\text{eff},L}\tau_{\eta}}\right)^{2}\sigma_{u1}^{2}\right]^{-1} (225)
  3. 3.

    Compute non-adopter objects:

    TA∗\displaystyle T_{A^{*}} =τd+τA+τlearn\displaystyle=\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\text{learn}}
    Δ\displaystyle\Delta =TA∗−1−TL−1\displaystyle=T_{A^{*}}^{-1}-T_{L}^{-1}
    Σp\displaystyle\Sigma_{p} =τp,L−1\displaystyle=\tau_{p,L}^{-1}
    τeff,A∗\displaystyle\tau_{\text{eff},A^{*}} =[Δ+(Σp|σd,L2)]−1=[Δ+Σp​σd,L2Σp+σd,L2]−1\displaystyle=\left[\Delta+(\Sigma_{p}\,|\,\sigma_{d,L}^{2})\right]^{-1}=\left[\Delta+\frac{\Sigma_{p}\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}{\Sigma_{p}+\sigma_{d,L}^{2}}\right]^{-1}
  4. 4.

    Compute inattentive objects:

    σd,I2\displaystyle\sigma_{d,I}^{2} =TI−1+σξ2\displaystyle=T_{I}^{-1}+\sigma_{\xi}^{2}
    τeff,I\displaystyle\tau_{\text{eff},I} =σd,I−2\displaystyle=\sigma_{d,I}^{-2}
  5. 5.

    Compute aggregates: S=mL​τeff,L+mA​τeff,A∗+mI​τeff,IS=m_{L}\tau_{\text{eff},L}+m_{A}\tau_{\text{eff},A^{*}}+m_{I}\tau_{\text{eff},I}, wj=mj​τeff,j/Sw_{j}=m_{j}\tau_{\text{eff},j}/S

  6. 6.

    Read off coefficients (a,b,g,χ)(a,b,g,\chi) from the formulas above

This sequential procedure yields an equilibrium characterization without iterative fixed-point computation. The rational expectations consistency condition is satisfied because beliefs are formed correctly given the price function, and the price function correctly aggregates demands given beliefs.

Step 6: Efficiency and comparative statics. An increase in the proportion of adopters (ϕ\phi) or the quality of their information (τη\tau_{\eta}) makes the price more informative about the private signal η\eta. The mechanism operates through the noise-to-signal ratio:

χg=α​TLV​mL​τeff,L​τη\frac{\chi}{g}=\frac{\alpha T_{L}}{Vm_{L}\tau_{\text{eff},L}\tau_{\eta}} (226)

Effect of adoption rate (ϕ\phi): As ϕ\phi increases, mL=ϕ​πAm_{L}=\phi\pi_{A} increases, which directly reduces (χ/g)(\chi/g). Intuitively, more LLM adopters trading on their private signal η\eta makes the price more informative about η\eta relative to the noise.

Effect of LLM quality (τη\tau_{\eta}): As τη\tau_{\eta} rises, TLT_{L} increases linearly in the numerator, while the denominator τeff,L⋅τη\tau_{\text{eff},L}\cdot\tau_{\eta} grows faster, ensuring χ/g\chi/g falls (making prices more informative). The strength of this effect depends critically on the relative magnitude of payoff noise σξ2\sigma_{\xi}^{2} versus fundamental uncertainty TL−1T_{L}^{-1}. When payoff noise is small (σξ2≪TL−1\sigma_{\xi}^{2}\ll T_{L}^{-1}), the effect is dramatic: σd,L2≈TL−1\sigma_{d,L}^{2}\approx T_{L}^{-1} shrinks rapidly with τη\tau_{\eta}, creating a quadratic relationship τp,L∝TL2\tau_{p,L}\propto T_{L}^{2} that causes adopters to trade very aggressively on their superior signal. The denominator τeff,L⋅τη\tau_{\text{eff},L}\cdot\tau_{\eta} grows approximately like τη3\tau_{\eta}^{3}, so χ/g∝τη−2\chi/g\propto\tau_{\eta}^{-2} falls rapidly. Conversely, when payoff noise is large (σξ2≫TL−1\sigma_{\xi}^{2}\gg T_{L}^{-1}), the effect saturates: σd,L2≈σξ2\sigma_{d,L}^{2}\approx\sigma_{\xi}^{2} remains nearly constant, capping both fundamental precision and speculative trading intensity. In this regime, χ/g\chi/g remains a decreasing function of τη\tau_{\eta}, but the effect saturates as τη→∞\tau_{\eta}\to\infty: χ/g\chi/g approaches a positive constant. Intuitively, large irreducible payoff noise limits how aggressively agents can trade on any signal, thereby limiting the informativeness of prices.

Both channels increase the learning precision:

τlearn=[ση2+(α​TLV​mL​τeff,L​τη)2​σu​12]−1\tau_{\text{learn}}=\left[\sigma_{\eta}^{2}+\left(\frac{\alpha T_{L}}{Vm_{L}\tau_{\text{eff},L}\tau_{\eta}}\right)^{2}\sigma_{u1}^{2}\right]^{-1} (227)

Since market efficiency is increasing in the precision with which agents can forecast the fundamental, and non-adopters’ forecast precision is TA∗=τd+τA+τlearnT_{A^{*}}=\tau_{d}+\tau_{A}+\tau_{\text{learn}}, market efficiency improves as ϕ\phi or τη\tau_{\eta} increase. This creates strategic complementarity: as more agents adopt superior LLMs, prices become more informative, benefiting even non-adopters through the information aggregation mechanism. This feedback effect can support partial adoption equilibria where some sophisticated investors rely on price discovery rather than directly acquiring the technology. ∎

Online Appendix E: Interpretability Methodology

To analyze heterogeneity in information processing across different types of news, we develop a technique involving topic modeling and linear regression. For topic modeling, we employ BERTopic [29], a topic modeling approach that combines modern embedding techniques with clustering algorithms. This method enables us to categorize headlines into coherent semantic categories without imposing predefined topic structures.

Sample and Data Preparation

Our analysis focuses on overnight news headlines with directional GPT-4 predictions (excluding neutral scores of 0), yielding 81,700 observations. We preprocess the headlines by removing the prediction labels (‘YES,’ ‘NO’, or ‘UNKNOWN’) from GPT-4’s explanations to avoid mechanical clustering based on these markers rather than underlying news content.

Technical Implementation

The BERTopic pipeline consists of five steps:

1. Sentence Embeddings.

We transform each headline into a dense vector representation using the SentenceTransformer model [59]. Specifically, we employ the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model from Hugging Face, which maps text to a 384-dimensional embedding space where semantically similar headlines cluster together.

2. Dimensionality Reduction.

We apply UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection; [56]) to reduce the embedding dimensionality from 384 to 5 dimensions while preserving both local and global structure. We use standard UMAP parameters: 15 neighbors and minimum distance of 0. This step concentrates semantic similarities in a lower-dimensional space to enhance clustering performance.

3. Initial Clustering.

We apply K-Means clustering to identify initial groupings of headlines in the reduced embedding space. We set K=50 clusters as the initial partition, which provides sufficient granularity to capture fine-grained distinctions in news content while maintaining adequate cluster sizes for analysis.

4. Topic Reduction.

To facilitate interpretation and statistical power, we reduce the 50 initial clusters to 20 final topics using BERTopic’s hierarchical topic merging algorithm. This algorithm iteratively merges the most similar topics based on their c-TF-IDF representations until reaching the target number. This reduction step consolidates semantically related clusters while preserving the major thematic categories in the data. The final 15 topics range from large categories like “Insider Stock Transactions” (16,790 headlines) to smaller but distinct categories like “Retail Store Openings” (175 headlines).

5. Topic Labeling.

After identifying the final topics, we generate human-interpretable topic labels using GPT-4o. For each topic, we extract representative headlines and keywords, then prompt GPT-4o to create a concise, descriptive label. The prompt instructs the model to avoid firm-specific names and generic terms, focusing instead on the underlying business action or market event common across headlines in each topic. The specific prompt is as follows:

You are tasked with extracting a short but highly descriptive topic label from a topic model and a set of example documents from that topic.

The documents contain [DOCUMENT TYPE].

Follow these instructions carefully:

1. Review the following documents: [DOCUMENTS]

2. Consider the following keywords that describe the topic: [KEYWORDS]

3. Based on the information provided in the documents and keywords, extract a short but highly descriptive topic label.

a. Keep the label at most 4 words long.

b. Do NOT include specific names, firm names, or stock tickers in the label, as the examples may come from only a few companies.

c. Interpret the concise topic rather than focusing on specific entities.

d. Make the label MORE specific than general terms like ‘Financial Results’, ‘Earnings Announcement’, ‘Financial Announcements’, ‘Financial Updates’, or ‘Corporate Finance Announcements.’

e. Avoid using firm names in whole or in part, tickers, and the words ‘Quarterly’ or ‘Financial’ in your label.

f. Focus on the specific theme that best describes the collection of explanations and keywords.

Keep your topic label concise, specific, and descriptive.

Provide your final topic label in the following format: topic: <<topic label>>

Methodological Advantages

This approach offers several advantages over traditional topic modeling methods (e.g., Latent Dirichlet Allocation) for our purposes. First, the embedding-based approach captures semantic similarity better than bag-of-words representations, which is particularly important given the brevity and density of news headlines. Second, K-Means clustering ensures all headlines are assigned to topics (no outliers), which maximizes sample utilization for our statistical analysis. Third, the two-stage approach (initial K-Means followed by hierarchical merging) balances granularity and interpretability: we capture fine-grained semantic distinctions in the initial clustering, then consolidate them into interpretable categories. Fourth, reducing to 20 final topics provides sufficient statistical power per category while maintaining conceptual coherence. Finally, using GPT-4o for labeling ensures consistency with our broader analytical framework while maintaining human interpretability of the resulting categories.

The resulting topic assignments enable us to decompose GPT-4’s performance and market reactions across 15 distinct categories of corporate news, as presented in Table 4 of the main text. Table OA6 below provides the complete list of topics with their representative keywords and example headlines. In the regression analysis underlying the decomposition table, we do not include firm or date fixed effects to preserve topic interpretability, but standard errors remain double-clustered by firm and date to account for potential correlation in residuals.

Online Appendix F: Transaction Cost Analysis

This section presents a comprehensive analysis of transaction costs and portfolio turnover for drift-based trading strategies. We examine strategies that enter positions after news announcements and exit after one trading session, focusing on the post-announcement drift component of returns.

1. Methodology

We analyze drift returns (ret_o) which measure the post-announcement price adjustment:

  • •

    Overnight News: For news released before 9 a.m. or after 4 p.m., we enter at market open and exit at market close, capturing the open-to-close drift return.

  • •

    Intraday News: For news released during trading hours (9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m.), we enter at market close and exit at the next day’s close, capturing the close-to-close drift return.

To address concerns about high turnover, we implement partial rebalancing strategies where the portfolio weight at time tt is:

wt=x⋅wt∗+(1−x)⋅wt−1w_{t}=x\cdot w^{*}_{t}+(1-x)\cdot w_{t-1}

where wt∗w^{*}_{t} is the target weight, wt−1w_{t-1} is the previous weight, and x∈{1.0,0.5,0.25}x\in\{1.0,0.5,0.25\} is the rebalancing fraction.

Importantly, partial rebalancing reduces both turnover and portfolio exposure. When targets change rapidly, positions converge only partway toward each new target before it changes again. For example, if the target flips from +100% long to -100% short, full rebalancing (x=1.0x=1.0) immediately shifts to -100%, while 50% rebalancing (x=0.5x=0.5) moves to 0% on day 1, then -50% on day 2. If targets continue changing, positions perpetually lag behind. In steady state, 50% rebalancing achieves approximately 100% gross exposure (50% long + 50% short) versus 200% for full rebalancing (100% long + 100% short).

Transaction costs are modeled as a fixed cost per round-trip trade, measured in basis points. We test cost levels of 0, 5, 10, and 20 basis points, which span the range from highly sophisticated investors to retail traders. We use fixed round-trip costs rather than bid-ask spreads because our baseline trades execute at the opening and closing auctions, which are call auctions that establish a single clearing price with no bid-ask spread. For overnight news released before 9 a.m., we enter at the opening auction and exit at the closing auction of the same day. For news released after market close, we enter at the next day’s opening auction and exit at that day’s closing auction. Because these auction mechanisms involve no continuous bid-ask spread, fixed costs parsimoniously capture commissions and price impact.

2. Results

Tables OA7 and OA8 present a comprehensive analysis of overnight and intraday news strategies, respectively. Each table reports: Sharpe ratios (Panel A), mean daily returns (Panel B), turnover and gross exposure (Panel C), and daily return volatility (Panel D) for both equal-weighted (EW) and value-weighted (VW) portfolios under different rebalancing intensities and transaction cost assumptions.

Panel C shows both average daily one-way turnover and average gross exposure (sum of absolute long and short positions). This dual reporting clarifies the fundamental trade-off: reducing rebalancing from 100% to 50% cuts turnover in half (from  190% to  94%) but also cuts gross exposure in half (from  196% to  101%).

The reduction in gross exposure from partial rebalancing has proportional effects on both mean returns and volatility, leaving Sharpe ratios relatively unchanged. For overnight news with equal-weighting at zero transaction costs, reducing rebalancing from 100% to 50% cuts mean daily returns approximately in half (from 0.34% to 0.17%) while also cutting volatility approximately in half (from 1.80% to 0.91%, Panel D). Because both mean and volatility scale proportionally with exposure, the Sharpe ratio remains nearly constant (2.97 for 100% rebalancing vs 2.95 for 50% rebalancing). This explains why Panel A shows minimal Sharpe ratio differences across rebalancing intensities at zero costs, despite the substantial differences in mean returns (Panel B) and volatility (Panel D): partial rebalancing reduces signal exposure but maintains similar risk-adjusted returns per unit of exposure.

3. Turnover and Transaction Costs

Panel C shows that the 100% rebalancing strategy exhibits extremely high turnover of approximately 190% per day for overnight news and 174% per day for intraday news.4141 41 In Figure OA3, we show the daily number of stocks held in the long and short legs of the overnight news strategy over time. The strategy holds an average of 74 stocks in the long leg and 21 stocks in the short leg per day, with substantial day-to-day variation reflecting fluctuations in news availability and sentiment. Additionally, Figure OA4 shows portfolio turnover for that strategy over time. Reducing the rebalancing fraction to 25% decreases turnover to approximately 45% per day for both strategies—a reduction of approximately 76%.

Panel A demonstrates that high turnover makes the 100% rebalancing strategy highly sensitive to transaction costs. For overnight news, the equal-weighted Sharpe ratio falls from 2.97 (zero costs) to -0.39 with 20 basis points costs. In contrast, the 25% rebalancing strategy is more robust, with its Sharpe ratio declining from 2.89 to -0.21 under the same cost assumptions.

Panel B shows mean daily returns under different cost levels. The 100% rebalancing strategy generates mean daily returns of 0.34% for overnight news at zero costs, but becomes unprofitable (-0.04%) at 20 basis points costs. The 25% rebalancing strategy shows more gradual performance degradation, maintaining positive returns up to 10 basis points costs.

4. Equal-Weighted vs Value-Weighted Portfolios

To assess whether the predictability is concentrated in smaller or larger stocks, we compare equal-weighted (EW) and value-weighted (VW) portfolios. In VW portfolios, stocks are weighted by lagged market capitalization (me_lag), giving more weight to larger firms.

The results show dramatically lower performance for VW portfolios:

  • •

    Overnight news (100% rebalancing, 0 bps costs): EW Sharpe = 2.97 vs VW Sharpe = 0.56

  • •

    Intraday news (100% rebalancing, 0 bps costs): EW Sharpe = 2.63 vs VW Sharpe = 1.28

The substantially lower Sharpe ratios for VW portfolios confirm that the predictability is heavily concentrated in smaller stocks. This finding is consistent with limits-to-arbitrage theories: smaller stocks face higher transaction costs and less attention from institutional investors, allowing mispricings to persist longer.

Notably, VW portfolios also show higher sensitivity to transaction costs. The overnight VW strategy becomes unprofitable even at 5 basis points costs (Sharpe = -0.40), while the EW strategy remains highly profitable (Sharpe = 2.13) at the same cost level. This occurs because the VW strategy concentrates capital in larger positions that face higher price impact costs.

5. Implications for Tradability

This analysis demonstrates that while the GPT-4 signal generates significant predictability, exploiting it requires careful attention to implementation costs. The 25% rebalancing strategy provides a more realistic alternative that:

  1. 1.

    Reduces daily turnover by approximately 76% (from  190% to  46% for overnight news)

  2. 2.

    Achieves approximately 28% of full signal exposure ( 54% gross exposure vs  196%)

  3. 3.

    Maintains similar risk-adjusted returns (Sharpe ratio) per unit of exposure

  4. 4.

    Shows more gradual performance degradation as costs increase

  5. 5.

    Remains profitable at moderate cost levels (5-10 basis points)

The comparison between EW and VW portfolios reveals that predictability is concentrated in smaller stocks, consistent with limits-to-arbitrage theories. While this concentration raises concerns about practical tradability for large institutional investors, it also validates the economic mechanism: markets are less efficient precisely where arbitrage is most costly.

6. Understanding the Size Effect: Reaction vs Drift

To understand why predictability concentrates in smaller stocks, we decompose returns into initial reaction (ret_n) and subsequent drift (ret_o) across market capitalization terciles (i.e., small, medium, and large caps). Tables OA9 and OA10 present this analysis.

The key finding is a striking asymmetry in drift patterns following negative news. Table OA9 Panel B shows that after stocks receive negative GPT-4 signals:

  • •

    Small caps: Initial reaction of -2.33% followed by drift of -0.70% (continued decline)

  • •

    Medium caps: Initial reaction of -1.34% followed by drift of -0.18% (modest continuation)

  • •

    Large caps: Initial reaction of -1.12% followed by drift of +0.06% (mean reversion)

This pattern explains the value-weighting underperformance. The short side of the strategy profits from drift continuation after negative news, which occurs for small and medium caps but not for large caps. Table OA10 confirms this at the portfolio level: short-only strategies achieve Sharpe ratios of 3.17 for small caps versus -0.61 for large caps.

In contrast, positive signals (Panel A) show positive drift across all size groups, though with declining magnitude for larger stocks. This explains why long-only portfolios perform reasonably well across all sizes (Sharpe ratios ranging from 0.30 to 1.09), while short-only portfolios exhibit dramatic size dependence.

The asymmetric drift patterns suggest different market mechanisms operate for positive versus negative news, and these mechanisms vary systematically with firm size. Large cap stocks experiencing negative news appear to benefit from support mechanisms—perhaps informed buying, liquidity provision, or analyst attention—that cause prices to partially recover. Small-cap stocks lack these support mechanisms, allowing negative drift to continue as uninformed investors gradually process the information.

This size-stratified analysis provides direct evidence for the mechanism behind the EW versus VW performance gap. It is not merely that smaller stocks are more predictable overall; rather, the predictability operates asymmetrically, with the short side working only for smaller stocks that exhibit drift continuation rather than mean reversion following negative news.
